title_en: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
title_fa: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
excerpt_en: Lenders don't want SpaceX shooting their collateral into orbit. What does that mean for space data centers writ large?
excerpt_fa: Lenders don't want SpaceX shooting their collateral into orbit. What does that mean for space data centers writ large?
content_en:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

content_en:
A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, which have dropped to new lows.
Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
From AirPods to Apple Watches, many Apple devices are already seeing notable discounts ahead of November 27th.
From AirPods to Apple Watches, many Apple devices are already seeing notable discounts ahead of November 27th.
Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of.
Featured Products
Earbud and headphone deals
AirPods Pro 3
The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.
Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.
- You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review.
- The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.
Beats Studio Pro
The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
- If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are down to $79.99 ($120 off) at Target in pink and white through November 22nd, marking a new low price. Amazon also has the pink headphones on sale for $79.99, while other colors are $20 more at both retailers. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.
- The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review.
MacBook deals
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
- The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,249 ($150 off) — a new low price — at Amazon and Best Buy. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Air (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
- The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,849 ($150 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price. title_en: Nothing's AI device debuts December 8, and it looks like two vapes stuck together
title_fa: Nothing's AI device debuts December 8, and it looks like two vapes stuck together
excerpt_en: Thanks, Swedish House Mafia. I guess.
excerpt_fa: Thanks, Swedish House Mafia. I guess.
content_en:
Nothing's AI device debuts December 8, and it looks like two vapes stuck together
Thanks, Swedish House Mafia. I guess.
In classic Carl Pei fashion, Nothing has begun to trickle out details about its latest product. On Friday the company shared that it plans to officially debut the new "AI-native device" with "no new screen and an experience that couldn't have been built as an app," on December 8. And if that was all there was to report, we probably wouldn't be publishing this story, but a photo of gadget has lazily drifted across social media like a fat cloud of fruit-flavored nicotine, thanks an unlikely source. Drink it in:
@nothing pic.twitter.com/WgcWNI2dIc
— Sebastian Ingrosso (@Ingrosso) November 19, 2026
On Wednesday at 10:28PM ET, Sebastian Ingrosso of house music trio Swedish House Mafia posted a photo on social media with Nothing's official X account tagged. Between a pair of Nothing Headphone 1 Pro headphones and a MacBook Pro, we can see a device that clearly fits the description of a screenless gadget like the one described by Nothing. "Bro... y u leak?" one X user wrote in response to the Ingrosso's photo. Is this a coordinated marketing stunt by Nothing? (Yes, duh.) Decide for yourself.
The one thing I can't get over is the fact that it looks like two vapes put together. Judging from the teaser the company shared, it also has at least one camera, likely for some kind of visual intelligence feature. We'll reserve judgment until we see the new device in person, but right now it looks like a rare miss by Nothing's design team.
Joking aside, it will be interesting to see how Nothing positions this device; the track record for AI gadgets isn't exactly encouraging. Humane went out of business at the start of last year, and Rabbit has sort of plodded along ever since the debut of the R1.

excerpt_en: Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.
excerpt_fa: Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.
content_en:
You can reveal the full GTA 6 map in minutes using this simple plane trick
Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.
GTA 6 has a huge map, which is around twice as big as the one found with GTA 5. That's a whole lot of Florida-inspired strip malls and alligator-soaked swamps. However, new players start the game in a fairly remote region, based on the Florida Keys, and the vast majority of the map is unavailable for perusal.
Fog is obscuring every part of the map that you haven't explored yet. New regions get uncovered as you travel through them. You could do this the long way, by following the story. You could also do this the slightly-shorter way, by grabbing a car and just driving north until the wheels fall off. GTA 6 doesn't have a system in place that automatically ups the wanted level as you enter new areas, so that's good.
However, the quickest way to unlock the full map is found in the skies, and not the roads. Long-time players know the drill. Jason needs to get an airplane.
Finding a plane
Luckily, there's a plane just a few miles north of Jason's first house in Key Lento. Take a break from making home renovations and head to Southpoint Airfield, as seen in the map above. It's basically just north of the starting area.
Drive the western bridge that runs over the Shoeless Keys and then head west a little bit onto a runway. It's hard to miss. The area is marked as restricted, but it's mostly abandoned so there shouldn't be any armed onlookers.
Once at the airfield, look for a duster plane just waiting to be flown. Hop in and do your thing. Planes move incredibly fast and will quickly unlock all of those foggy areas. Just fly carefully and keep an eye on fuel.
You probably won't be able to get the whole map done on a single fly through, due to that fuel, but planes automatically regenerate at airfields as soon as one leaves. Fly back to Southpoint and start again, this time heading in another direction. You'll have the whole map uncovered in minutes.
Happy travels. The only real thing to worry about here is the Mile Zero Air Station at the bottom left of the map. Flying over that airspace will instantly generate a four-star wanted rating. This wanted level can bring police after you in helicopters, so airplanes aren't necessarily safe. Save this area for last and exit as soon as the fog lifts from the map. Mile Zero is home to some really fast aircraft, but it's likely not worth the trouble just yet.

title_en: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
title_fa: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
excerpt_en: Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as "a modern take on a classic CD player" with its new EP/BC-1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC-1 is the...
excerpt_fa: Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as "a modern take on a classic CD player" with its new EP/BC-1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC-1 is the...
content_en:
Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”
Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp.
Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.
If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

title_en: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
title_fa: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
excerpt_en: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics's most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world's best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark...
excerpt_fa: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics's most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world's best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark...
content_en:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

title_en: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
title_fa: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
excerpt_en: If you're wondering how Alex Ridha's (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn't. That's not to say Ridha didn't learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but...
excerpt_fa: If you're wondering how Alex Ridha's (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn't. That's not to say Ridha didn't learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but...
content_en:
If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge.
Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
‘I always look for the newest machines.’
“I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”
On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”.
“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.
He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.
But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”
Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

title_en: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
title_fa: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
excerpt_en: Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it looks like Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
excerpt_fa: Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it looks like Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
content_en:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

title_en: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
title_fa: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
excerpt_en: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
excerpt_fa: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
content_en:
A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.
The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.
According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.
The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.
Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.
Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”
From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.
Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.
Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.
“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”
“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.
The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.
It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.
“Basic human error”
Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.
The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.
Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.
“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.
Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.
Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.
“Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”

title_en: Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) review: Minor upgrades that cost too much
title_fa: Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) review: Minor upgrades that cost too much
excerpt_en: Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.
excerpt_fa: Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.
content_en:
Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) review: Minor upgrades that cost too much
Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.
You'd be forgiven if you came out of Meta Connect feeling like Meta's third-generation Ray-Ban glasses seemed like a bit of an afterthought. The latest model was announced alongside the company's new audio-only glasses, its first VR glasses and an updated lineup of cheaper Meta-branded frames.
Compared with other recent glasses from the company, there's not that much new to report. Meta's latest Ray-Ban glasses have gotten some cosmetic updates and a few performance upgrades around the edges. There's still a lot to like; the frames are the most premium Meta-branded smart glasses without a display. But considering just how many variations of frames the company now makes, it's not clear that the $449 Gen 3 glasses should be your default choice if you're looking to invest in a new pair.
New frame styles and details
For now, the third-gen Meta Ray-Ban glasses only come in three frame styles: there's the classic Wayfarer frames, which have gotten a bit slimmer; Zena, a new cat-eye shape and Aviator, which Meta says is a tribute to the classic Ray-Ban design. As usual, each style is available in a number of different frame colors, many of which are semi-transparent so you can see some of the inner components if you look closely.
For this review, I wore a pair of Aviator frames in a brown tortoiseshell color called Havana. I've spent a lot of time in previous reviews complaining about glasses only coming in dark, boxy frames, so I was excited to see two new shapes. But it is disappointing that both the Zena and Aviator frames start at an eye watering $529.
Maybe it's because the new, bolder frame shapes aren't for everyone. I've owned many aviator-style sunglasses over the years, but these felt the most oversized. They are 10mm wider than the smallest Gen 3 Wayfarer frames and it definitely showed on my face. I also felt a little silly wearing thick aviator glasses with clear lenses. I understand Meta offers clear transition lenses as the default choice for most of its AI glasses because it gives people more flexibility in how they wear them. But I think this particular frame shape is better suited to sunglasses.
The bulkiness of the frames also caused some issues with the fit. The glasses constantly slipped down my nose to the point where I considered buying after-market silicon tips to keep them in place. The glasses' tips are technically adjustable, but unlike some other Meta Glasses that offer DIY adjustments, Ray-Ban Meta frames need to be adjusted professionally by an optician or at a Meta store. That's not a big deal if you buy a pair at one of these physical establishments, but it's kind of a pain if you order online.
The other major noticeable change with Gen 3 is the addition of the action button, which has appeared on other recent models of Meta glasses. It's basically a customizable shortcut that lets you trigger a specific action without a voice command. I like to set mine to "read my latest text message," but you can use it for just about any Meta AI query.
Under the hood, Gen 3 comes with two upgrades compared with Gen 2. It has a slightly better battery life, with the frames lasting "up to 9 hours" on a single charge and the charging case adding an additional 50 hours. That's about an hour better than Gen 2, but as usual, battery life can vary significantly depending on how you use them. I was able to squeeze about six hours of continuous audio playback on my pair. Features like Live AI, which uses the camera to analyze your surroundings, will drain the battery even more quickly.
Gen 3 also comes with an extra microphone, which Meta says should improve the sound quality for phone and video calls you take with your glasses. I never got any complaints with the five-mic setup on Gen 2, but people I spoke to on the phone while wearing Gen 3 assured me that I sounded clearer than I do on my AirPods Pro 2.
Meta AI + what's to come
The latest glasses come with all the same Meta AI features as the rest of the company's lineup. The AI assistant is now powered by Muse Spark, which has generally made conversations feel more natural and reduced errors. I do miss the celebrity voices, though.
Speaking of voices, Meta has made it clear that its smart glasses will be even more important to the company as its AI agent Muse advances. The company previewed Muse on its glasses during Connect, but the feature hasn't officially rolled out yet, though a Meta support page describes it as being in "beta." Once Muse is available on the device, you'll be able to chat with your agent via your glasses and "show" it what you're seeing through the glasses' cameras. That obviously opens up a lot of interesting possibilities, though it's hard to say how big of a deal this will actually be.
I also worry that Muse and other AI features are likely to become a vehicle for Meta to more aggressively hawk Meta One subscription plans. The company has already shown a willingness to paywall some features, like its new hearing enhancement tool (which has yet to roll out). The company also seemingly considered a similar move with its other hearing-related feature Conversation Focus, which also has yet to fully roll out despite being announced more than a year ago.
And when I look at my own glasses settings, the very first menu I see is a promotion to sign up for Meta One in order to unlock more photo storage. The company is, officially, still "testing" these subscription plans, but it does raise important questions about future enshittification.
One setting I am grateful to have is the ability to opt out of allowing the company to train its AI models on "visual data" collected by your glasses. That means that when you ask Meta AI a question about something you're looking at, the glasses will not store that image and won't show it to contractors the company employs. That addition...

title_en: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
title_fa: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
excerpt_en: From notetakers to webcams, here are six AI-powered gadgets to upgrade your workspace.
excerpt_fa: From notetakers to webcams, here are six AI-powered gadgets to upgrade your workspace.
content_en:
Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.
From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159)
If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.
The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.
You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.
The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
Anker Soundcore Work ($159)
Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work, is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.
Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.
The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.
If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).
Logitech MX Keypad ($99)
Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.
The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.
Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($479)
Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.
Starting at $479, the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.
Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.
Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249)
If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.
Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.
The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.
Autonomous Desk Pro ($499)
Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.
Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.
The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

title_en: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
title_fa: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
excerpt_en: Elon Musk may have been overstating it when he said Nvidia’s employees “love” the ousted Jensen Huang.
excerpt_fa: Elon Musk may have been overstating it when he said Nvidia’s employees “love” the ousted Jensen Huang.
content_en:
Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”
Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people.
According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.
Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

title_en: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
title_fa: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
excerpt_en: "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," California AG Rob Bonta said.
excerpt_fa: "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," California AG Rob Bonta said.
content_en:
California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.
The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.
The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).
The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.
The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.
The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

title_en: Google boosts Gemini's ability to do 'repetitive tasks' on its Mac app
title_fa: Google boosts Gemini's ability to do 'repetitive tasks' on its Mac app
excerpt_en: Google's Gemini app for Mac can now use your computer to list items on eBay, speed up creative tasks and fill out forms for you.
excerpt_fa: Google's Gemini app for Mac can now use your computer to list items on eBay, speed up creative tasks and fill out forms for you.
content_en:
Google boosts Gemini's ability to do 'repetitive tasks' on its Mac app
The feature can list multiple items on e-commerce platforms for you, among other things.
Google's Gemini app for Mac now has the ability to do repetitive tasks on its own. The feature has been available to PC users for a while, but now the Mac app can also access Gemini's "Computer Use" capability. That means it can now see what's on your screen via screenshots, as well as click, type, scroll and navigate programs and websites for you. You can use the capability to automate tasks that would usually take several steps across programs and devices, as long as you tell Gemini what to do in natural language.
The AI app will work on your tasks in a background window and will just give you a live preview in your chat. It will not be taking control of your screen or your cursor, so you can use your Mac computer like you always do. Of course, Gemini will only be able to use the apps and programs you've given it access to, and it will ask for your approval for key actions.
In Google's announcement, it gave several examples for how you can use the new capability. You can use it to list items for sale on platforms like eBay in batches. If you're selling a whole bunch of clothes, for instance, you can ask Gemini to go through the photos you took of them stored in a local folder, research their pricing, log their details and then stage their listings. You can use it to quickly fill out local PDFs, such as shipping declaration forms. You can also use it to speed up creative work, such as getting Gemini to automatically turn a pencil sketch into a 3D model.

title_en: WhatsApp's group chats can now have up to 1,500 members
title_fa: WhatsApp's group chats can now have up to 1,500 members
excerpt_en: WhatsApp is giving users the ability to create even bigger group chats with up to 1,500 participants.
excerpt_fa: WhatsApp is giving users the ability to create even bigger group chats with up to 1,500 participants.
content_en:
WhatsApp's group chats can now have up to 1,500 members
The Meta-owned app has increased their limit from 1,024 participants.
WhatsApp has started rolling out the capability to add up to 1,500 participants to a single group chat, as reported by WABetaInfo. You might be thinking right now, "who in the world wants to be in a chaotic group chat with 1,499 other people?" We'd agree, but the new capacity could be very useful for administrators who handle chats for schools and local communities.
The app previously had a participant cap of 1,024 people in one chat. If a community has a larger number of people, the administrator may have to create another group. The new capacity could be large enough to serve their needs. WABetaInfo says the new participant limit will be available on both Android and iOS apps, but since the Meta-owned chat app is gradually rolling it out, some people may not be able to access it until later. It's not clear if chats with 1,500 people in them can use "audio hangouts," WhatsApp's Discord-like voice feature, from the start. But suffice it to say, you can expect those calls to be wild, confusing and noisy.
WhatsApp also recently released new features for group chats that sound especially useful for large groups. Users will now be able to pin messages for a longer period and to filter conversations by mentions and replies. In addition, old participants within the group will now be able to share their message history with anybody new the admin adds.

title_en: The Trump administration has replaced its cybersecurity chief
title_fa: The Trump administration has replaced its cybersecurity chief
excerpt_en: The White House has replaced cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross with the Pentagon's Kirsten Davies.
excerpt_fa: The White House has replaced cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross with the Pentagon's Kirsten Davies.
content_en:
The Trump administration has replaced its cybersecurity chief
Sean Cairncross was ousted following several high-profile tech outages.
Sean Cairncross is no longer the US National Cyber Director. The Trump administration has fired him, following several tech outages in the country, according to Reuters. If you'll recall, Microsoft's services recently went down and remained offline for almost a full day, which had affected businesses, hospitals and even governments around the world. The Federal Aviation Administration had also ordered a nationwide ground stop that had disrupted more than 18,000 flights inside, to and from the US.
It's not quite clear why the White House removed Cairncross in relation to those incidents, but the government has been getting flak over its response to cybersecurity threats, including those posed by advanced AI agents and tools. Cairncoss oversaw the administration's cybersecurity strategy, as well as the implementation of related policies across the federal government. According to Axios, however, Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, wanted him out because he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The president, "fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," Reuters' source said.
In a statement, Cairncross said he was proud of what he had done "to strengthen America's cyber security, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in super intelligence."
Kirsten A. Davies, the Department of Defense's chief information officer, will now serve as the new US National Cyber Director. Davies had held cybersecurity-related posts in the private sector before, including in companies like Hewlett-Packard and Siemens. The administration reportedly believes she has the experience and the credentials needed to be able to excel in the position.

title_en: The U.S. national cyber director is stepping down
title_fa: The U.S. national cyber director is stepping down
excerpt_en: The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.
excerpt_fa: The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.
content_en:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.
Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.
We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

title_en: OpenAI is testing Dots personal agents on its $20 per month Plus tier
title_fa: OpenAI is testing Dots personal agents on its $20 per month Plus tier
excerpt_en: OpenAI is expanding access to Dots, the proactive AI agents that can work for you without any supervision or assistance.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI is expanding access to Dots, the proactive AI agents that can work for you without any supervision or assistance.
content_en:
OpenAI is testing Dots personal agents on its $20 per month Plus tier
Dots are also coming to all ChatGPT Business Standard users starting today.
OpenAI is expanding access to Dots, the proactive, always-on AI agents that can toil at tasks for you without any supervision or assistance. After launching the feature for higher-tier plans from ChatGP Pro and up, the company announced that it's testing Dots with a small number of users on the cheaper $20 per month ChatGPT Plus plan.
"Heads up, we're starting to test dots with a small number of ChatGPT Plus users," OpenAI's ChatGPT engineering lead Thibault "Tibo" Sottiaux wrote on X. "Looking forward to the continued feedback as we expand and I'm recently seeing a lot more positives around how good the proactivity has been after many improvements."
Heads up, we're starting to test dots with a small number of ChatGPT Plus users. Looking forward to the continued feedback as we expand and I'm recently seeing a lot more positives around how good the proactivity has been after many improvements.
We're also bringing dots to all...
— Tibo (@thsottiaux) November 19, 2026
Dots can interact with over 4,000 apps thanks to their access to OpenAI's plugin ecosystem. The agents can work autonomously on tasks and make progress even when you don't interact with them. They can even connect to your PC, allowing them to control it on your behalf and work alongside you. You can check up on their progress by opening a Dot's "computer" at any time.
Along with limited availability on ChatGPT Plus, Dots are coming to all ChatGPT Business Standard users starting today, Tibo said. For higher-tier plans, conversations with the agents don't count toward regular ChatGPT usage limits for Pro and Business Premium subscribers, as long as they don't involve complex tasks. It's not clear, though, if Plus or Business Standard users will get that benefit as well.
Originally powered by GPT-6 Astra, Dots can now run on GPT-6.1 Terra as well. The company just launched several new features for them as well, including iOS widgets and Shortcuts integration, along with iMessage and RCS support, plus iOS notification replies. If you're on a Plus plan, you may gain access starting today, but OpenAI has yet to say whether the upgrade will be permanent.

title_en: Uber Kids will let parents book trips for their children aged 10 to 12 years old
title_fa: Uber Kids will let parents book trips for their children aged 10 to 12 years old
excerpt_en: Uber is testing rides for children ages 10 to 12 and will pay drivers more for them.
excerpt_fa: Uber is testing rides for children ages 10 to 12 and will pay drivers more for them.
content_en:
Uber Kids will let parents book trips for their children aged 10 to 12 years old
It's a limited pilot program available in just three locations for now.
Uber is giving parents and guardians the option to get their kids a special ride they can track and monitor, at least in a few specific locations. The ride-hailing company has started testing a new service called Uber Kids meant for children aged 10 to 12 years old. According to TechCrunch, it rolled out quietly in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee and Madison, Wisconsin over the past weeks.
The company already has Uber for Teens, but that program lets teenagers aged 13 to 17 make bookings from their own accounts, as long as they're part of a Family profile with a parent or guardian. For Uber Kids, only parents and guardians can order a ride for their children, and they must be present at pickup. Like on rides taken by teens, they'll also be able to access live video feed from inside the car to check in on their child in real time. Guardians themselves can come on the trip, along with additional minors, as long as they have their own parents' or guardians' permission. However, multi-stop rides aren't allowed on Uber Kids, and all trips booked under the program must be to a single destination.
Uber isn't sending Kids ride requests to all drivers on its network. The company is only inviting highly rated drivers to participate in the program, and those interested will have to complete a short course to be able to get in. They will also be required to enable audio and video recordings on their app, as well as to switch on camera and microphone access so that guardians can watch their kids on the ride. Uber says drivers will be notified once Live Video starts and that only the kids' guardians and safety agents will be able to access the realt-time feed.
Since Kids rides come with all these requirements, Uber will pay drivers $7 more compared to a standard UberX trip. Drivers will also get an additional $20 for the first Kids trip they complete. As TechCrunch notes, though, this is just a limited pilot program, and it's not clear if the company has plans to expand it to more locations in the future.

title_en: Google's latest home page redesign makes Gemini even more prominent
title_fa: Google's latest home page redesign makes Gemini even more prominent
excerpt_en: Google is doubling down on Gemini AI in its desktop search, despite complaints from users and employees alike.
excerpt_fa: Google is doubling down on Gemini AI in its desktop search, despite complaints from users and employees alike.
content_en:
Google's latest home page redesign makes Gemini even more prominent
A new collapsible sidebar in AI mode shows your most recent searches.
Google is doubling down on Gemini AI in its desktop search, despite protestations from users and employees alike. The latest feature is a collapsible sidebar in AI mode that shows your most recent searches, in case you want to jump back to a previous query. "In testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress and continuing to explore the web," wrote VP of search Robby Stein on X.
The new sidebar is only available in Google Search's AI mode. Clicking anywhere on the left of the AI search window opens up the sidebar, showing all recent searches, both AI and organic. Then, selecting any of the sidebar descriptions opens up an AI mode search window on the subject. You can close the AI search sidebar at any time by clicking on the "close sidebar" icon at the top right.
New on the Google desktop homepage globally: we're rolling out a collapsible sidebar to easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches.
People are coming to Search with more questions that aren't just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for... pic.twitter.com/mKHz295tzK
— Robby Stein (@rmstein) November 19, 2026
If you're like me and never use Google's dedicated AI Search mode, you won't see the new sidebar. Still, it's bound to ruffle some feathers among users and publishers who think there's already too much Gemini in Google Search. (As an, er, sidebar, I'd add that the feature would be nice to have in regular Search, as a list of recent queries would save me from having a zillion tabs open.)
Google seems to value its AI search development more than actual money, given that its market cap recently dropped by $500 billion after it admitted that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search. However, the company is likely focused on maintaining its AI search lead over rivals like ChatGPT and Claude. And, as CEO Sundar Pichai put it in the company's last earnings call, Google's commitment to AI is "long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise."

title_en: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
title_fa: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
excerpt_en: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
excerpt_fa: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
content_en:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”
“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

title_en: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
title_fa: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
excerpt_en: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
excerpt_fa: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
content_en:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.
At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.
Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.
However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”
With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.
$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.
Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.
Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.
28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.
The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.
More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.
Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.
All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

title_en: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
title_fa: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
excerpt_en: On the day Anthropic went public, Fireworks AI’s co-founder made the case for open source models as a cheaper alternative, and addressed the breaches that have cost the company some customers’ trust.
excerpt_fa: On the day Anthropic went public, Fireworks AI’s co-founder made the case for open source models as a cheaper alternative, and addressed the breaches that have cost the company some customers’ trust.
content_en:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion.
Fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.
Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.
Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.
There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity.
You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?
When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?
I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
How far behind are open models right now?
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?
Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?
We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.
Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.
On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?
Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?
I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?
Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so...
